podcast.title: Dave Gahan's Near-Death Experience and Recovery (1995-1996)
podcast.body: From late spring 1995 through to a brief clinical death in 1996, Dave Gahan's life was consumed by heroin addiction, costing $3,000 daily, leading to extreme dissociation, conversations with stuffed animals (including a Bugs Bunny doll), and two suicide attempts. On May 27, 1996, after an attempt to record with Martin Gore, Gahan injected cocaine and heroin at the Sunset Marquis Hotel in Hollywood, leading to full cardiac arrest and two minutes of clinical death. He recalled a vision of his wife screaming for him to return and a voice stating, "This is wrong, you don't get to decide." His recovery began after summer 1996, largely influenced by the threat of green card revocation from the American government if he didn't enter rehab and remain sober. He has been sober since June 6, 1996, now runs four times a week, lives in New York's West Village, and is married to Jennifer, his third wife. "He was for all intents and purposes clinically dead for two full minutes. He now says he remembers the vision of his wife screaming at him to come back to this plane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Suicide Attempts and Overdose (1995-1996)
podcast.body: While staying at the Sunset Marquis hotel in August 1995, Dave Gahan attempted suicide by slashing his wrists in the bathroom mirror. After waking in a psychiatric ward, his primary focus was getting high again, seemingly indifferent to the fact that a suicide attempt was a felony in California. He later made another unsuccessful attempt to hang himself in his bathroom. His struggles culminated on May 27, 1996, when after attending a party and checking back into the Sunset Marquis, he injected a mixture of heroin and cocaine, resulting in a massive overdose. At 1:15 AM on May 28, an unknown person called 911, and paramedics found him clinically dead for two minutes due to full cardiac arrest. "When he woke up in the psychiatric ward, all he could think about was getting high again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Clinical Death and Court-Ordered Rehab (1996)
podcast.body: On May 27th, 1996, after working on new material in New York, Gahan returned to Los Angeles, checked into the Sunset Marquis, and injected a potent mix of heroin and cocaine. He suffered a massive overdose, was found clinically dead for two minutes by paramedics at 1:15 AM on May 28th. After being released from the hospital, he immediately used drugs again but experienced no high. A court-ordered stay at the Exodus Recovery Center in Los Angeles appeared to finally establish his sobriety, which has reportedly continued ever since. "When paramedics arrived, Dave had been clinically dead for two minutes."

podcast.title: Near Dissolution and Reforming (1996)
podcast.body: Following Alan Wilder's departure in 1995, the remaining members, Andy Fletcher and Martin Gore, began working on new material in 1996. During this time, Dave Gahan's severe heroin addiction made recording with him nearly impossible, leading to serious discussions about expelling him from the group, finding a new singer, or even Martin Gore embarking on a solo career with Ultra potentially becoming his first solo album supported by Fletcher. The band's future was truly uncertain. "Ahí ya fue cuando prácticamente se llevaba plantear la disolución y que ultra fuese el primer disco hecho ya en la carrera Martin Gorko con el apoyo de Andrew Fishery."

podcast.title: Post-Overdose Recovery (1996)
podcast.body: Following his release from the hospital and subsequently from jail on drug charges after his massive overdose in May 1996, Dave Gahan immediately returned to using heroin ("smack"). However, this time, he experienced no "buzz" or effect from the drug. This profound lack of sensation prompted him to voluntarily admit himself to the Exodus Recovery Center in Marina del Rey, California, a facility notably known for having treated Kurt Cobain shortly before his death. At Exodus, Gahan embraced accountability for his actions, achieved sobriety, cleaned up, and has reportedly maintained a clean and straight lifestyle since late 1998. "But this time, there was no buzz. There was nothing."

podcast.title: Long-Term Recovery and Current Status (1997-Present)
podcast.body: Depeche Mode eventually overcame the tumultuous period between 1991 and 1997. Dave Gahan and Martin Gore are now sober, and Alan Wilder is living a quiet life. While Andy Fletcher died in 2022, Martin Gore and Dave Gahan continue to record and tour together, showing intent to move forward almost 50 years after the band's formation. "The good news is that the Pesh mode eventually came out on the other side of all things that happened between 1991 and 1997."

podcast.body: Like many other rock stars, Andy Fletcher experienced problems with anxiety and depression, developing a severe case of OCD in his early 20s which worsened after his sister's death. podcast.title: Andy Fletcher's Quiet Demeanor
podcast.body: Andy Fletcher was known as the "quiet one" in Depeche Mode, content to let Dave Gahan and Martin Gore handle most of the speaking during interviews. "Andy was the quiet one in Depeche Mode."

podcast.body: Martin Gore resides in Santa Barbara, California, where his ex-wife owns a spa. Dave Gahan lives in New York, and Andrew Fletcher has his home in the Maidstone area of London. "So we got Martin living in California. There's Dave in New York and Andrew in London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Name Origin and Mis-translation
podcast.body: The name "Depeche Mode" was adopted from a French fashion magazine. For many years, it was commonly, but incorrectly, translated as "fast fashion." The more accurate translation, reflecting the spirit of the original French, should be "fashion news update." "Your name depech mode was taken from the title of a French fashion magazine. I heard that. And for years, that has been wrongly translated as fast fashion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band's Enduring Longevity
podcast.body: Despite a tumultuous history filled with personal struggles, lineup changes, and extreme touring conditions, no one involved with Depeche Mode – including the band members, their record company, management, or families – can believe that the band is still together. "No one, including the band, their record company, their management, and their families can believe that after all this, the Peshmo is still together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Biggest Selling Technopop Band
podcast.body: Depeche Mode became Mute Records' most successful signing and ultimately the biggest-selling band to emerge from Britain's Technopop era. Their worldwide sales today are "somewhere north of 100 million." "Depeche Mode eventually became the biggest selling band to emerge of the whole Technopop era in Britain. And today, worldwide sales, somewhere north of 100 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Blend of Technopop and Industrial
podcast.body: Depeche Mode was positioned as a band "caught right in the middle" of the Technopop and industrial scenes, known for being polite and innocuous Technopop while their songwriter, Martin Gore, was influenced by aggressive industrial acts. This blend led to the incorporation of industrial elements into their music. "Depeche Mode is a great example. They were caught right in the middle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Influence on Depeche Mode
podcast.body: Depeche Mode showed clear influences of David Bowie's work, particularly in the realm of goth music and electronic sounds. Bowie's legacy as a pioneer in electronic and genre-bending music resonated with bands like Depeche Mode. "You could see lots of Bowie influence in Depeche Mode and the cure and new order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cause of Death: Aortic Dissection
podcast.body: Andy Fletcher's cause of death was an aortic dissection, a rare condition that is seldom diagnosed in advance due to few warning signs and can result from factors like high blood pressure or congenital conditions, leading to rapid internal bleeding. "Cause of death was an aortic dissection, a rare condition that's almost never diagnosed in advance because there's no real reason to look for it because there are a few, if any, warning signs."

podcast.body: Dave Gahan once sported a "gesh," a piercing in the area behind the scrotum, which he believed was the most erotic place to be pierced, despite its pain and discomfort. He eventually removed it after one of his children innocently questioned its presence during a shower. "He once had something called a geesh, GEISH, a geesh. This is a piercing of the area. It's the behind the scrotum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Gahan's British Display Society Award
podcast.body: After three years of art college, Dave Gahan earned a British Display Society Award, qualifying him to design store display windows. This provided a practical skill should his music career ever falter. "After three years, he ended up with something called a British Display Society Award. Which means if the singing thing ever falls through, he has qualified to design display windows for stores."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Gahan's Embrace of Rock God Persona
podcast.body: During the "Songs of Faith and Devotion" tour, Dave Gahan fully adopted a "rock god" image, which was visibly expressed through changes in his hairstyle and the acquisition of additional tattoos. One notable tattoo on his shoulder blades required a painful ten-hour session to complete. "Dave had totally embraced the rock god thing by this point. We saw changes in hairstyle, more tattoos, including one on his shoulder blades that took 10 painful hours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Gahan's First Divorce and Remarriage
podcast.body: Following a personal crisis, Dave Gahan left his first wife, Joanne, with whom he had a young son named Jack and had been married since the mid-1980s after knowing each other since their teenage years. He subsequently moved to Los Angeles, where he became romantically involved with Teresa Conway, Depeche Mode's former press officer, which resulted in the birth of a baby daughter. Gahan divorced Joanne and later married Teresa at the Graceland Chapel in Las Vegas, where an Elvis impersonator provided the wedding music. "Dave divorced Joanne and married Teresa at the Graceland Chapel in Las Vegas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Gahan's Paranoia and Delusions
podcast.body: Amidst his severe drug addiction, Dave Gahan developed extreme paranoia, leading him to carry a gun even for routine tasks like walking from his house to the mailbox. His mental state deteriorated into delusional behavior, including watching the Weather Channel for 24 consecutive hours, painting his walls and floor black, and engaging in conversations with his collection of stuffed animals, a behavior that became concerning when he claimed the animals began to speak back to him. "He grew paranoid and carried a gun, even just to get from the house to the mailbox."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Gahan's Parental Issues
podcast.body: Dave Gahan's childhood was affected by parental issues; his parents divorced when he was three, and his mother remarried. His stepfather was presented as his biological father until Dave discovered the truth at age 10, which profoundly impacted him. "Dave has had some issues regarding his parentage when he was three his parents divorced and his mom remarried. Stepdad was then present to Dave as his real dad. Stayed that way until he was 10, which is when he found out the truth, and that really messed him up for a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Gahan's Second Marriage and Tattoo
podcast.body: Dave Gahan married his second wife, Teresa Conway, at the Graceland Chapel in Las Vegas, with an Elvis impersonator providing the music. As a pledge of love, Dave commissioned a tattoo reading "TC TTM/FG," which stands for "Teresa Conway to the motherf***ing Gahan." "Dave Gahan married his second wife Teresa Conway at the Graceland Chapel in Las Vegas. The music for the service was provided by an Alvison personator as part of Dave's pledge of love. He had a new tattoo commissioned yet rent TC TTM slash FG. It stands for Teresa Conway to the mother Blanker Gahan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Gahan's Stalker Incident
podcast.body: Dave Gahan faced extreme fan intrusion due to Depeche Mode's massive success, prompting him to move homes twice after repeatedly waking to fans singing on his lawn. In one alarming instance, a fan hired a private detective to track Gahan from the recording studio to his house to discover his address. "Dave had already moved twice because he kept waking up to find the Peshmoan fans singing on his front lawn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dave Gahan's Teenage Delinquency and Art College
podcast.body: As a teenager, Dave Gahan appeared in juvenile court three times for offenses like car theft and vandalism, and he held 20 different jobs within six months. His enrollment in art college was the only thing that saved him from a path of delinquency. "As a teenager, he went to juvenile court three times, for things like stealing cars and vandalism. He went through 20 different jobs in just six months."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decadent Tour Staff and Incidents
podcast.body: The "Songs of Faith and Devotion" tour employed approximately 100 individuals, including a dedicated full-time psychiatrist and a staff member specifically tasked with procuring drugs. During this tour, several band members experienced severe issues: Martin Gore suffered two grand mal seizures and numerous panic attacks, Andrew Fletcher endured a mental breakdown so severe that doctors initially suspected a brain tumor, and keyboardist Alan Wilder ultimately quit the band. "The tour employed a hundred people, including a full-time psychiatrist and a guy whose job it was to buy drugs."

podcast.body: Detecting the risk of an aortic dissection typically requires advanced imaging such as a CT scan, MRI, or ultrasound, as there is no other way to tell if one is in danger. "but unless you have a CT scan or an MRI or an ultrasound, there's no way to tell if you're in danger."

podcast.title: Dominant Songwriting Role
podcast.body: Martin Gore has consistently been the chief songwriter for almost all of Depeche Mode's material since 1982's A Broken Frame, continuing to the present. "If you care to check the credits on pretty much every album from a broken frame in 1982 to the present, you'll see that it's been pretty much all about Martin."

podcast.title: Dressing Room Arrangements on Tour
podcast.body: On the road, Martin Gore and Andrew Fletcher share a dressing room, while Dave Gahan has his own. This arrangement is primarily attributed to Dave's need to avoid the temptations of backstage life. "When they're on the road, Martin and Andrew share a dressing room. Dave gets his own. That always more to Dave's need to be away from the temptations of backstage life than anything else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drug Dealer on Tour (Songs of Faith and Devotion Tour)
podcast.body: Despite the presence of a psychiatrist, the 120-member staff on the "Songs of Faith and Devotion" tour also included a drug dealer. This individual was responsible for supplying members like Dave Gahan with cocaine and heroin, directly counteracting the psychiatrist's efforts to provide counseling for drug issues. "But then again, that 120 member staff also included a drug dealer to make sure that guys like Dave Gahan were well supplied with cocaine and heroin."

podcast.title: Early 80s Alt Rock Example
podcast.body: This band is cited as an example of early 1980s Alt Rock, characterized by its use of synthesizers and a "fancy name," which The Smiths deliberately contrasted with their own plain naming convention and guitar-driven sound. Like The Smiths, they also provided solace to troubled, sensitive, shy, and alienated music fans. "Because back in the early 80s, Alt Rock was all about synthesizers played by bands with fancy names like orchestral maneuvers in the dark and de Pesh mode."

podcast.title: Early 80s Androgynous Makeup
podcast.body: In the early 1980s, Depeche Mode was influential in popularizing androgynous makeup styles among male musicians. This aesthetic contributed to the diverse visual landscape of the new wave era. "Styles run from the over-the-top glam of David Bowie and the New York Dolls in the early 1970s to the androgynous styles of Depeche mode in the early 80s..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 90s Struggles
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, Depeche Mode was in a "very bad place" largely due to extensive drug and alcohol use. Martin Gore suffered severe seizures, leading doctors to suspect a brain tumor. Andy Fletcher (Fletch) experienced debilitating panic attacks, and keyboardist Alan Wilder quit the band due to the stress. Singer Dave Gahan was heavily addicted to heroin and cocaine. "In the early 90s, Depeche Mode was in a very bad place. Thanks to lots and lots and lots of drugs and alcohol."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Live Performances with Tape Machines
podcast.body: In early Depeche Mode videos, reel-to-reel tape machines are prominently displayed, used to play back pre-recorded rhythm tracks during live performances. This practice was common in the techno pop era before more sophisticated drum machines and sequencers became widespread for live use. "You can see one in some early-to-pech mode videos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Eclipsing Shoegaze
podcast.body: During the mid-1980s, while new Shoegaze bands were forming, established acts like Depeche Mode continued to release major albums, which somewhat overshadowed and eclipsed the nascent Shoegaze movement. "Durante mitad de los 80 seguíamos teniendo grandísimos discos de Bandage como de Depech Mode, de Reem, de DeCure, que un poco iban equilipsando a esta nueva generación."

podcast.body: Ultra is considered by many to be Depeche Mode's most emotional and intimate album, serving as a raw reflection of the personal struggles and eventual healing of its members. The album vividly captures Martin Gore's sadness, aggression, and exhaustion from years of personal battles, alongside Dave Gahan's physically deteriorated state and his remarkably sad, decadent, and subdued vocal performances, all indicative of the profound personal challenges they faced. "Es un álbum emocionalmente muy intimista porque tenemos aquí yo creo que los dos grandes momentos emocionales de los osotabonistas completamente plasmados."

podcast.title: Enduring Influence in the 90s
podcast.body: While Technopop declined in the 1990s, elements of synth pop continued to resonate and live on in their music. "it did, however, live in some respects in the music of nine-inch nails, de Pesh mode, radio head, and Bjork."

podcast.title: Evolution of Instrument Use
podcast.body: Guitars and real drums have periodically fallen in and out of favor with Depeche Mode; there was a significant period in their career where their sound was 100% electronic and synthesized. In their very early days in the late 1970s, guitars were part of their sound but were seen as restrictive and logistically difficult to transport compared to synthesizers. "One we felt that guitars restricted us. The sound of the guitars very limited. And we found synthesizers very interesting, just the sounds that you could get on them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Example of Diverse Alternative Music
podcast.body: Depeche Mode was presented as an example of "electronic pop" within the "alternative" genre, demonstrating the wide variety of sounds that fell under this umbrella term. The "alternative" label could encompass their electronic sound as much as low-fi guitar rock. "Alternative could be anything from low-fi, fuzzy guitar rock from a band like Sonic Youth, to some electronic pop from Depeche Mode."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Explicit Political and Social Themes in *Spirit*
podcast.body: The *Spirit* album delves into political and social themes, influenced by recent global political changes, which is a continuation of topics from previous works. However, in *Spirit*, this discourse is notably "more evident and explicit" than what fans were previously accustomed to. "Este discurso político nos deja cosas son tanto más evidentes y explícitas de lo que estábamos acostumbrados."

podcast.title: Extensive 12-inch Remixes (80s-Early 2000s)
podcast.body: Depeche Mode singles were known for being remixed in a dozen different ways specifically for nightclubs during the 80s, 90s, and early 2000s. podcast.title: Extensive Remix Catalog
podcast.body: Depeche Mode is noted for its deep involvement in remixing, to the extent that completists require significant shelf space for their collection. A box set of selected remixes released between 1981 and 2004 contained 37 different remixes of 37 different songs, and another box set released in 2016 featured 28 additional remixes. There's also a vinyl "suitcase-like collection" spanning half a dozen discs, illustrating the band's prolific output of remixed material. "I have on my shelf a box set of selected Dopech Mode Remixes released between 1981 and 2004, 37 different remixes of 37 different songs. And next to it is another box set released in 2016 with another 28 remixes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Flood's Engineering Work
podcast.body: Before becoming a renowned remixer and producer, Mark Price (known as Flood) worked as an engineer at Mute Records, contributing to sessions for bands like Depeche Mode. "Eventually he got a job as an engineer at mute records, working sessions for bands like DePesh Mode."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gasconi – Andy Fletcher's London Italian Restaurant
podcast.body: Andy Fletcher of Depeche Mode, along with his wife Grania, opened an Italian restaurant called Gasconi in the mid-1990s in the St. John's Wood area of London, near Abbey Road recording studios and Violet Hill. The restaurant, located at one Blenheim Terrace, was intended as a distraction for Andy due to the adverse effects of Depeche Mode's extensive touring, which had caused him to miss part of a tour previously. It became a pilgrimage site for Depeche Mode fans, and Martin Gore, the band's songwriter, was a frequent visitor. Andy eventually sold his stake in Gasconi to focus on his record label, Toast Hawaii, and occasional DJ gigs. "Gasconi was supposed to be something that could distract him between Depeche Mode projects."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Goth Influence and Success
podcast.body: Depeche Mode, though not originally or truly a Goth band, became influenced by Goth music as the 1980s progressed, leading to significant record sales and, for many new fans, a path back to Goth itself. "as the 1980s wore on, they were influenced by this music and ended up selling a gazillion records as a result."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Handshake Contract with Mute
podcast.body: Depeche Mode famously operated for years with Mute Records without a formal contract. Their relationship was based on a simple handshake agreement. "They never really signed a formal contract with Mut. For years, the relationship honestly existed on nothing more than a handshake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Heroin Addiction Development
podcast.body: Dave Gahan initiated heroin use around 1991, rapidly progressing to a full-blown addiction by 1993. His residence in Los Angeles significantly exacerbated his drug problem, as drugs were easily accessible, especially after his second wife, Teresa, introduced him to the social circle associated with Jane's Addiction. "He had started using heroin in about 1991 and two years later he was a full-blown addict."

podcast.title: Hipster's Favorite Hit Makers
podcast.body: By the end of the 80s, as Anglo-Files turned away from "Big 80s pop," bands like Depeche Mode became "hipster's favorite hit makers" on alternative radio and the modern rock chart. "do me new waivers like the Cure, The Smiths and Depeche Mode became hipster's favorite hit makers."

xref.title: Band Name Origin

xref.body: Perry Bamonte, brother of Daryl Bamonte (who filled in for Depeche Mode), started his career as a guitar tech for The Cure. "Perry Bimonte, the brother of the affirmation Darrell Bimonte who bailed out Depeche mode in 1994 started as a guitar tech for the cure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

xref.title: Happy, Naive Worldview
xref.body: Similar to Depeche Mode, the band was characterized by a happy, almost naive worldview, reflecting a more optimistic second wave of electronic music. "And like Depeche Mode, they had a happy, almost naive worldview."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

xref.title: Influence on Martin Gore (Depeche Mode)
xref.body: Martin Gore, the songwriter for Depeche Mode, listed Einstürzende Neubauten among the industrial bands he listened to in his spare time, indicating their significant influence on his musical development and later work with Depeche Mode. "And of course, Einstein's Andy Neubaden. This aggressive approach to music really appealed to Martin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influenced by Industrial Bands
xref.body: As the songwriter for Depeche Mode, Martin Gore privately listened to aggressive industrial acts such as Fad Gadget (known for using power drills), Test Department (known for performances in quarries and car factories), and Einstürzende Neubauten. This exposure led him to incorporate industrial elements into Depeche Mode's music as he gained more control. "But if you would ask songwriter Martin Gore, who he listened to in his spare time, he would have listed names like Fad Gadget, the group that liked to use black and decker power drills in their music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Legal Battle with TVT Records
xref.body: Trent Reznor endured a significant and "protracted legal battle" with TVT Records after label head Steve Gottlieb expressed disdain for Nine Inch Nails' music, reportedly calling Pretty Hate Machine "an abortion," despite expecting a Depeche Mode-like electronic act. This dispute legally prevented Reznor from recording any music under his name or as Nine Inch Nails, leading him to participate uncredited in side projects like 1000 Homo DJs. "What followed was an ugly and protracted legal battle that kept Trent Rezner from recording anything under his name or as Nine Inch Nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: If That Is Your REAL Name

xref.title: Long Incubation Period for Solo Debut
xref.body: It took Dave Gahan 22 years to release his first solo album while being a member of Depeche Mode. "It took him 22 years to get around to it. But at least he did it, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Long-time Road Crew Member for Depeche Mode
xref.body: Daryl Bamonte had been a part of Depeche Mode's road crew since the early days of the band, indicating a deep familiarity with their operations and music. "His place was taken by Darrell Bomonte, who had been working as part of Depeche modes road crew since the early days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

xref.title: Model, Writer, Spiritualist, Musician
xref.body: Andrea Hogan, a German-born musician, was a former model who wrote horror movies, supported the Goth scene, and was a poet and pagan spiritualist. She worked under various names, including Hügellands Roondance, exploring genres from ambient and electronic to rock, industrial, and black metal. She was also friends with musicians like Martin Gore of Depeche Mode. "Andrea was a former model who wrote horror movies and supported the Goth scene. She was a poet and pagan spiritualist. She was also a musician who worked under a variety of names and a variety of genres, ranging from ambient and electronic to rock industrial and even black metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Music as Escape and Teenage Influences
xref.body: Following a football injury that sidelined him for much of a season, music became Scott Weiland's primary escape. His favorite bands during this period included Depeche Mode, The Clash, Social Distortion, The Sweet, Echo & The Bunnymen, and Queen. "Music became his escape, especially after a football injury forced him to sit out much of a season."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Musical Beginnings and Influences
xref.body: Trent began piano lessons at age five and later learned to play the tuba and saxophone in the school band. He was fascinated by bands like Supertramp and Pink Floyd, as well as anything related to the Antichrist. His primary inspiration for becoming a musician, surprisingly, came from synth-driven bands like The Human League, OMD, and Depeche Mode, which he found "really cool" compared to punk bands like the Sex Pistols, The Clash, and The Ramones. "The piano lesson started at age five. He learned to play the tuba and the saxophone in the school band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

xref.title: Musical Influences
xref.body: The Bravery incorporated elements from Depeche Mode, The Cure, Echo & the Bunnymen, The Cars, and Duran Duran to create a sound that felt both new and familiar. Their music, released in 2005, prompted rhetorical questions about whether it was from 2005 or 1980. "They took bits of Depeche Mode, the cure, echo in the bunnyman, the cars, and Durand-Dorand to come up with something new yet very familiar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

xref.title: Musical Influences
xref.body: Bennington cited Scott Weiland of Stone Temple Pilots and Dave Gahan of Depeche Mode as his musical heroes, though the transcript notes these were "not exactly guys whose lifestyle should be emulated." "Although his heroes were Scott Wyland of the Stone Temple Pilots and Dave Gahn of Depeche Mode, not exactly guys whose lifestyle should be emulated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opening Act on Devotional Tour
xref.body: Miranda Sex Garden opened for Depeche Mode on the Devotional Tour but quit after a particularly bad show where the audience pelted them with rotten meat and dog excrement. "One of the bands who opened for Depeche Mode on this tour was a group called Miranda Sex Garden. They quit the tour after the audience pelted them with rotten meat and dog excrement after one particularly bad show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Personal Life and Outside Projects (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Alan Wilder got married and purchased a 30-acre, eight-bedroom estate in the English countryside. He also pursued projects outside Depeche Mode, working with a group called Recoyl and the English Electronic Body Music (EBM) band, Knights of Rab. "He got married and bought a 30-acre eight-bedroom estate in the English countryside."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour

xref.title: Pioneering 80s Keyboard-Bass Alt Rock
xref.body: Duran Duran was also mentioned as a "keyboard bass band" from the 1980s, whose music was central to the dance culture of alternative kids before grunge took over, and whose style saw a revival in the 2000s. "25 years earlier, long before Grunge guitars took over, alternative kids danced to keyboard bass bands like Depeche Mode, New Order, OMD, Durand Iran, the Human League, Eurasia, Eurythmics, and so many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering 80s Keyboard-Bass Alt Rock
xref.body: The Human League was recognized as one of the "keyboard bass bands" from 25 years before the 2000s that alternative kids listened and danced to, embodying the electronic and dance elements of 80s alt rock that saw a revival in the oughts. "25 years earlier, long before Grunge guitars took over, alternative kids danced to keyboard bass bands like Depeche Mode, New Order, OMD, Durand Iran, the Human League, Eurasia, Eurythmics, and so many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering 80s Keyboard-Bass Alt Rock
xref.body: Erasure was listed as a "keyboard bass band" from the 1980s, whose music was a staple for alternative kids dancing before the rise of grunge, and whose electronic dance attitude experienced a revival in the 2000s. "25 years earlier, long before Grunge guitars took over, alternative kids danced to keyboard bass bands like Depeche Mode, New Order, OMD, Durand Iran, the Human League, Eurasia, Eurythmics, and so many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering 80s Keyboard-Bass Alt Rock
xref.body: Eurythmics was identified as one of the "keyboard bass bands" from 25 years prior to the 2000s, whose music resonated with alternative kids and contributed to the dance-oriented electronic sound of 80s alt rock that later saw a resurgence. "25 years earlier, long before Grunge guitars took over, alternative kids danced to keyboard bass bands like Depeche Mode, New Order, OMD, Durand Iran, the Human League, Eurasia, Eurythmics, and so many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering 80s Keyboard-Bass Alt Rock (Electronic Revival)
xref.body: New Order was a significant "keyboard bass band" of the 1980s that alternative audiences danced to, and their sound served as an influence for the New Wave Revival. The band's style embodied the dancey electronic elements of 80s alt rock that experienced a resurgence in the 2000s. "Now you could tell by listening that these artists grew up listening to groups like Durand Oran, Joy Division, The Cure, New Order, Pixies, The Police and You too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Alt Rock Dance Scene (Mid-1980s)
xref.body: New Order was instrumental in the birth of the Alt Rock dance scene starting in the mid-1980s. They experimented with drum machines, samplers, and 12-inch remixes, helping to remove the stigma of disco and make dancing cool for fans of alternative music. "thanks to artists like New Order and Depeche Mode and the Cure experimenting with drum machines, samplers and 12 inch remixes, an Alt Rock dance scene was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

xref.title: Pioneering Alt Rock Dance Scene (Mid-1980s)
xref.body: The Cure contributed to the development of the Alt Rock dance scene in the mid-1980s by incorporating drum machines, samplers, and 12-inch remixes into their work. This helped establish a new cultural phenomenon where alternative rock fans actively engaged in dancing. "thanks to artists like New Order and Depeche Mode and the Cure experimenting with drum machines, samplers and 12 inch remixes, an Alt Rock dance scene was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

xref.title: Pioneers of 1980s Techno Pop
xref.body: Yazoo is mentioned as one of the groups central to the techno pop sound of the 1980s, alongside bands like Depeche Mode, Human League, and Visage. This era saw widespread adoption of synthesizers in popular music. "And this brings us to the techno pop sounds of the 1980s, to Pesh Mode, Human League, Yazoo, Visage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneers of 1980s Techno Pop
xref.body: Visage is highlighted as a key act in the development of 1980s techno pop, a genre characterized by the pervasive use of synthesizers. They are grouped with other influential bands like Depeche Mode, Human League, and Yazoo. "And this brings us to the techno pop sounds of the 1980s, to Pesh Mode, Human League, Yazoo, Visage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Depeche Mode Life (Present)
xref.body: Alan Wilder now lives quietly, having owned a 30-acre, eight-bedroom country estate with his own recording studio. He also possessed a vacation property in Vestfold, Norway. "Alan Wilder is living quietly."

xref.title: Prominent Technopop Band
xref.body: Eurythmics was listed among the Technopop bands that achieved popularity, further demonstrating the genre's crossover appeal into the pop charts and its exposure on platforms like MTV. "Petchop boys, Urythmix, Erasure, More Depeche Mode."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prominent Technopop Band
xref.body: Erasure was highlighted as a Technopop band that enjoyed significant popularity, contributing to the genre's presence on both alternative music stations and mainstream pop charts. "Petchop boys, Urythmix, Erasure, More Depeche Mode."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Provider of Comfort to Fans
xref.body: The Cure is mentioned as a band that, similar to Depeche Mode and The Smiths, offered something for troubled, sensitive, shy, and alienated music fans to "hang on to" and embrace for comfort. "Like to pesh mode in the cure, the Smiths gave troubled, sensitive, shy and alienated music fans something to hang on to."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

xref.title: Radical Remixes for Depeche Mode
xref.body: Adrian Sherwood created "pretty radical remixes" for Depeche Mode songs like "People Are People" and "Master and Servant," characterized by heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops. These remixes were highly influential, particularly on Al Jourgensen of Ministry. "Adrian had created some pretty radical remixes for Depeche Mode, most notably for people are people and master and servant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Relationship and Marriage to Teresa Conroy (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Dave Gahan became involved with Teresa Conroy, Depeche Mode's former press officer, who introduced him to the Jane's Addiction social circle where drugs were readily available. They were described as "rock and roll soulmates," indulging in the rockstar lifestyle and having a baby daughter together. They married at the Graceland Chapel in Las Vegas by an Elvis impersonator in April 1992. "He also hooked up with Teresa Conroy, the Pesh Mode's former press officer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Post-Punk Band
xref.body: After being inspired by an art rock band, Scott Weiland formed his own post-punk band named Soy DeSant. The French name, meaning "a style of one's own," was a nod to Depeche Mode, one of Weiland's favorite bands. "That inspired Scott to form his own post punk band that he called Soy DeSant, which translated means a style of one's own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Songwriting Dominance and Personal Challenges (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Martin Gore became the sole songwriter for Depeche Mode, which created tension with Alan Wilder. He claimed to be autistic and indulged heavily in partying and drinking, often withdrawing into video games like "Sonic the Hedgehog." Becoming a father for the first time in June 1991 added further stress. "He wanted to contribute more as a songwriter, but that had pretty much become the sole domain of Martin Gore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour

xref.title: Synth Experimentation and Production
xref.body: Giorgio Moroder, an Italian musician, was a pioneer in experimenting with new synthesizers as they emerged. His work, particularly his production of Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" in 1977, was highly influential, shaping the sound of disco with robotic, futuristic elements and inspiring countless electronic and technopop bands. Moroder's innovations drew a direct line to groups like Depeche Mode, OMD, and the Human League, and even inspired David Bowie, serving as a gateway to electronic music and Kraftwerk for many fans. "He had an extraordinarily big hit in 1977 with this song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Toured with Ministry's Early Band
xref.body: Culture Club toured with Alan Jourgensen's early Technopop band from Chicago, providing an early association for the artist who would later become a pioneer of industrial music. "Alan was in a Tectopop band from Chicago that had spent some time touring with both Depeche Mode and Culture Club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Trent Reznor's View
xref.body: Trent Reznor acknowledged punk bands like the Sex Pistols as "cool," but found the electronic sounds of synthesizers and drum machines from bands like The Human League to be "really cool," indicating a preference for synth-driven music. "Punk bands like the Sex Bistles and the Clash and the Remones were cool and everything. But the synthesizers and drum machines of the human league and OMD and Depeche mode. Now that was really cool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

xref.title: Trent Reznor's View
xref.body: The Clash were considered "cool" by Trent Reznor, but their punk rock sound was superseded in his personal inspiration by the synthesizers and drum machines employed by bands like The Human League. "Punk bands like the Sex Bistles and the Clash and the Remones were cool and everything. But the synthesizers and drum machines of the human league and OMD and Depeche mode. Now that was really cool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

xref.title: Trent Reznor's View
xref.body: Trent Reznor regarded The Ramones as "cool" within the punk genre. However, his musical inspiration was more profoundly shaped by the electronic elements of synth-pop bands, which he found "really cool." "Punk bands like the Sex Bistles and the Clash and the Remones were cool and everything. But the synthesizers and drum machines of the human league and OMD and Depeche mode. Now that was really cool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

xref.title: Unconventional Performance Venues
xref.body: Test Department was a group known for staging performances in unusual and industrial locations such as quarries and car factories, reflecting an aggressive approach to music that appealed to Martin Gore of Depeche Mode. "Then there was Test Department, a group we liked to stage performances in places like quarries and car factories."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Use of Power Drills in Music
xref.body: Fad Gadget was known for incorporating Black & Decker power drills into their music, an aggressive and unconventional approach that appealed to and influenced artists like Martin Gore of Depeche Mode. "Fad Gadget, the group that liked to use black and decker power drills in their music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Vince Clark's Post-Depeche Mode Project
xref.body: After leaving Depeche Mode, Vince Clark formed Yazoo, a project that achieved a series of hits and enjoyed considerable success for a period. "There was a group called Yazoo, what a series of hits."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Vince Clark's Post-Depeche Mode Project
xref.body: Eurasia was another musical project Vince Clark embarked on after his departure from Depeche Mode, enjoying a successful career on its own. "Then there was Eurasia, who had a nice little career on their own."
